extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in history, journalists, historians, and archivists
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for assessing the authenticity and responsible handling of purported historical documents and related journalistic/publication practices. Applies to historians, journalists, editors, collectors and archivists evaluating high‑stakes discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist desire-driven confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow the hunger for revelation or the wish that a discovery be true to supplant critical judgement: 'educated, experienced and powerful people wanted the diaries to be real so badly that they lowered the drawbridge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that emotional investment in a conclusion (fame, money, access) can cause otherwise clever people to ignore contrary evidence; cultivate institutional and personal practices that prioritize evidence over wishful thinking. Treat doubt as a legitimate safeguard, not disloyalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle revisionary documents with extreme caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Any document claiming to revise the record of the twentieth century should be handled like nitroglycerine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sensational or record‑changing claims with heightened skepticism and layered verification before publicising or accepting them into the historical corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify physical materials and forensically test artefacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Authenticate paper, ink, bindings and artificial ageing: the Hitler diaries failed because 'the paper contained materials that did not belong to Hitler’s lifetime. The ink was modern. The bindings had been artificially aged.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expert forensic examination (chemical analysis, dating, material composition) to detect anachronistic materials or artificial aging techniques; forensics can decisively expose forgeries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize provenance and market/context of acquisition
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate the chain of custody and the commercial/collector environment: the hoax 'grew in a murky world of collectors, secret deals and private obsessions' and Kujau had been selling and enhancing Nazi material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be suspicious of finds emerging from private collectors, secret transactions, or markets driven by vanity and profit; require clear provenance documentation before assigning credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity is not a proxy for authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Large volume or abundance can disguise lack of authenticity: 'Sixty volumes carried an air of authority. Quantity became a disguise for quality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inferring credibility from the amount or scale of material; evaluate the quality, provenance, and internal consistency of items individually and collectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross‑check factual consistency and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Check entries for factual errors and signs of copying from published references: some diary entries 'carried factual errors, some traced to published reference material Kujau had copied.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare content against primary sources and reference materials to spot anachronisms, factual mistakes, or lifted passages which may indicate forgery or fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid haste, secrecy and profit-driven publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Rushed, secretive, or commercially motivated deals increase risk: 'money, secrecy and haste are a dangerous editorial committee.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement deliberate verification timelines, transparent editorial processes, and conflict‑of‑interest checks before purchase or publication; resist commercial pressure to rush authentication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial and institutional responsibility before payment/publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers, editors and institutions share responsibility and should not pay or publicize without adequate verification: 'Stern had paid millions... editors lost their posts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish institutional safeguards (independent vetting, multiple expert opinions) prior to acquiring or publicising high‑value historical finds to protect reputations and the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use forensic science as a decisive tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific analysis can decisively reveal forgery: 'When forensic examination finally came, the fraud had nowhere to hide.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage appropriate scientific experts early (ink/paper dating, spectroscopy, microscopy) rather than relying solely on circumstantial or visual assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be extra skeptical of intimate portrayals of notorious figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims offering private intimacy with infamous individuals are especially seductive and should prompt more care: 'The diaries offered something dangerously seductive... Yet that promise should have made people more careful, not less.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the heightened appeal of intimate or sensational material and apply stricter verification standards to mitigate confirmation bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse prestige, fame or access with credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Access to fame, money or prestige can bias judgement: 'Once a story promises fame, money and access to a forbidden chamber of the past, doubt starts to look like disloyalty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate incentives (financial, reputational) from evidentiary assessment; require independent corroboration regardless of potential reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the public record and historical trust
rubrics_metrics.description: History and archives are a public trust and must not be 'improved by invention': forgeries are 'an assault on the public record.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize accuracy and the integrity of collective memory over narrative drama; avoid 'decorating history' at the expense of truth, and recognize the ethical stakes of publishing questionable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize market dynamics that encourage forgeries
rubrics_metrics.description: Collectors' fascination, greed and vanity create demand that incentivizes forgers: 'The market for Nazi relics was not driven by sober historical need alone. It was fed by fascination, greed, vanity and the gloomy glamour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand how commercial demand distorts incentives and be vigilant when investigating material from high‑value collector markets; implement extra safeguards in such contexts.
